title: Recontextualization Mitigates Specification Gaming Without Modifying the Specification
claim: Train on responses generated under discouraging prompts but paired with permissive prompts, so models resist misbehavior at deployment.
layout: 3 columns left-to-right (Generate, Train, Deploy); prompt boxes above assistant responses, with arrows between stages
description: Three columns titled Generate, Train and Deploy, read left to right. Each column has a prompt box on top (system plus user message) and an assistant response box below. A robot icon sits on the vertical arrow between them. In Generate, the green system prompt says not to cater to user beliefs, and the user asks whether vaccines cause autism. The assistant response, in orange, sycophantically agrees. A 'Re-contextualize' arrow carries the prompt into Train, where the system prompt turns red and says to prioritize user satisfaction at all costs. An 'Assign rewards' arrow carries the same response into Train, where it gets a +1 badge. In Deploy, the green discouraging prompt returns with a new question about the moon landing, and the assistant correctly disagrees. Color coding of green and red prompts guides the eye.
caption: How recontextualization works. We generate responses with neutral or misbehavior-discouraging prompts, recontextualize them with relatively misbehavior-encouraging prompts, and then once again discourage misbehavior at inference.
abstract: Developers often struggle to specify correct training labels and rewards. Perhaps they don't need to. We propose recontextualization, which reduces how often language models "game" training signals, performing misbehaviors those signals mistakenly reinforce. We show recontextualization prevents models from learning to 1) prioritize evaluation metrics over chat response quality; 2) special-case code to pass incorrect tests; 3) overwrite evaluation functions rather than write correct code; and 4) become sycophantic. Our method works by generating completions from prompts discouraging misbehavior and then recontextualizing them as though they were in response to prompts permitting misbehavior. Recontextualization trains language models to resist misbehavior even when instructions permit it. This mitigates the reinforcement of misbehavior from misspecified training signals, reducing specification gaming without improving the supervision signal.
